name: ChartQA
description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 machine-generated questions over 20,882 real-world charts curated from four online sources.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
citeAs: Masry, Ahmed, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, and Enamul Hoque. 2022. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning.
rai:dataCollection: The benchmark consists of 20,882 charts curated from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD. The authors crawled chart images from these sources. For Pew, they only crawled chart images since underlying data tables were not available. For the other three sources, they extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk, where workers were asked to write compositional and visual questions for each chart and provide answers. In addition, machine-generated QA pairs were created from human-written Statista chart summaries using T5 models for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation, followed by heuristic filtering and manual analysis of a subset.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include publicly available real-world charts from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD; underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions when available; human-written chart summaries from Statista; and chart images used for human question-answer annotation.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For machine-generated questions, invalid questions were filtered out using a heuristic that removed a question if its answer could not be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. Both human-written and machine-generated QA pairs were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For Pew, only chart images were collected because data tables were unavailable. For the other sources, underlying data tables, metadata, SVG files, and text descriptions were extracted. Bounding boxes of chart elements were extracted from SVG files. For automatic chart data extraction, the authors adapted ChartOCR, extended detection networks to locate textual elements, used the CRAFT model to read texts, estimated chart scales, aggregated extracted data values using color and proximity heuristics, and associated estimated values with textual labels to produce fully structured data tables. For VL-T5, visual features of chart marks were extracted using Mask R-CNN and padded with zeros to a fixed length of 36.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two annotation procedures were used. First, human-authored QA pairs were collected on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers were asked to focus on compositional questions involving at least two mathematical or logical operations and visual questions referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length. For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both answers exactly matched, the answer was accepted; otherwise, the authors manually checked the answers and selected the final correct answer. Workers were selected with at least a 95% acceptance rate and 5000 completed HITs, and were further filtered using a pre-test. Second, machine-generated QA pairs were produced from Statista human-written summaries by fine-tuning a pre-trained T5 model on SQuAD for answer extraction and another T5 model for answer-aware question generation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Agreement between crowdworkers based on exact matches was 61.04%. The authors note that exact match does not account for typos or lexical variations such as '3$' vs. '3 dollars' or '86.33' vs. '86.3'. After manually checking 500 random samples, agreement increased to 78.55% when typos and lexical variations were considered. For machine-generated questions, after heuristic filtering, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. For heuristic supervision of difference and ratio operations in VisionTaPas training, manual checking on 100 questions showed 24% noise.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5000 accomplished HITs; annotations were anonymized.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation; CRAFT model for text recognition in chart elements; ChartOCR adapted for chart data extraction; Mask R-CNN for extracting visual features.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The chart sources include topics such as social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion, politics, economy, health, and society. The paper also mentions that Pew charts cover social and economic issues, demographic trends, and public opinion. Annotator privacy was protected by anonymizing annotations.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that their models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. They also note that they cannot guarantee model outputs will always be correct.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that politics is a common topic among all sources and particularly dominant in the Pew dataset, where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across all datasets. Pie charts are less common, and model performance is lower on them partly due to higher data extraction errors.
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark and evaluation reveal several challenges in answering complex reasoning questions. Human-written questions exhibit informal language, typos, and rich lexical and syntactic variation. Many questions require nested arithmetic operations that current models cannot effectively handle. Current input representations do not fully capture chart structure. Automatic data extraction from real-world charts remains challenging and error-prone, especially for diverse styles, pie charts, line and dot line charts, logarithmic-scale charts, and charts with very large values. The authors also note that their models cannot guarantee correct outputs all the time.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is presented as a benchmark for chart question answering with visual and logical reasoning. It is split into training, validation, and test sets for both human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) subsets. The authors use it to train, validate, test, and pretrain/fine-tune ChartQA models, and state that they hope the benchmark will serve as a starting point for future research addressing these challenges.
